A message from the Dean

Opportunity
in motion

To our students, alumni, donors and friends: welcome to an issue about what becomes possible when an entire college moves opportunity forward together.

Throughout these pages, you will meet people who make the Zeigler College of Business distinctive. Students step into global companies, competitions, internships and working facilities. Faculty and directors create the conditions for those experiences to become meaningful. Alumni, advisors and industry partners bring the professions within reach.

Our theme, Opportunity in Motion, reflects that shared work. To our students: your curiosity and courage give these opportunities purpose. To our alumni and advisors: your time, insight and example help students imagine themselves in the work. To our donors: your generosity opens doors and helps more students walk through them prepared.

As Dean, I am proud that no single person stands at the center of these stories. Their strength comes from connection—across classrooms, campuses, careers and generations. Together, we are building more than a degree. We are building the confidence, judgment and relationships that help people contribute from their first day and continue growing long after graduation.

I hope you see your own place in this work and feel inspired by the momentum we are creating together.

Peter CampbellDean · Zeigler College of Business
University leadership · Commonwealth University

Leadership built
together

Dr. Jeffery L. Osgood, Jr. begins his presidency with a clear invitation: bring people together, listen with purpose and shape the university’s future as one community.

The PASSHE Board of Governors unanimously selected Osgood as president of Commonwealth University, effective April 17, 2026. The appointment builds on his service as interim president since August 2025, a period in which university leaders praised his collaborative approach, transparent communication and commitment to student opportunity.

That confidence was tested through a comprehensive search. Faculty, staff, students and system leaders participated in the process, which included 25 interview sessions across the university’s campuses and more than 200 pieces of community feedback. The Commonwealth University Council of Trustees also voted unanimously to recommend his appointment.

Osgood’s vision is grounded in trust, respect and shared purpose. He has emphasized the strength of students, the dedication of faculty and staff, the loyalty of alumni and the pride of the Bloomsburg, Lock Haven and Mansfield communities. For the Zeigler College of Business, that collaborative spirit offers an encouraging foundation: a university-wide culture where ideas move across roles and campuses, and where progress is work accomplished together.

Academic leadership · Commonwealth University

A steady hand
for what comes next

Commonwealth University’s people directory now lists Dr. Vanessa Kahen as Interim Provost and Senior Vice President for Academic Affairs—placing a student-centered, collaborative leader at the helm of the university’s academic enterprise.

Kahen brings more than 25 years of experience in public higher education to the role. At West Chester University, she served as Interim Dean of the Graduate School, Chair of Psychology and Director of Moon Shot for Equity. Across those assignments, her work joined strategic leadership with a clear concern for the people and partnerships that make institutional progress possible.

Her academic roots reinforce that perspective. Kahen earned a Ph.D. in Psychology from the University of California, Berkeley, and has built a leadership approach the university describes as relational, flexible and equity-minded. That combination—careful listening, creative problem-solving and an openness to change—offers an encouraging foundation for faculty, staff and students across Commonwealth’s campuses.

For the Zeigler College of Business, the transition is an opportunity to keep building across disciplines and locations: strengthening student success, supporting faculty work and connecting academic programs with the communities they serve. We look forward to working with Dr. Kahen as that shared work moves ahead.

At the same time, the college extends its warm appreciation to Dr. Michelle Kiec for her service as Provost and Senior Vice President for Academic Affairs. As she begins her new role, we wish her every success in the chapter ahead and thank her for the leadership she has given Commonwealth University.

Global business · Lead feature

Nine days.
One global classroom.

In Madrid, five international business majors learned that crossing a border changes more than the view. It changes the questions.

Led by Lam Nguyen, professor and chair of the Department of Management, the faculty-led trip paired cultural immersion with close study of global firms. At Herrero & Asociados, students examined how intellectual property becomes competitive strategy. At HM Hospitales, they considered how technology, service and innovation shape healthcare. At Sheffield Academy, they explored the professional value of cross-cultural fluency.

The itinerary kept moving between systems and settings. A session on Madrid’s role as a global business hub placed the city between Europe and Latin America; a collaborative case on online marketplace Letgo turned observation into analysis. Museums, civic institutions and public spaces added the political and cultural context in which markets operate.

Support from the University Foundation, Terry Zeigler, Tom Stiner, the Center for Global Engagement and university partners made the experience possible. That funding did more than underwrite travel. It gave Alexis Budline, Leydi Mueses Uillian, Tatiana Beckworth, Emma Holmes and Daytona Walter a working laboratory for adaptability.

Professional sales

Built for the conversation

Lexi Urbassik’s path from role-play to real work shows what happens when practice, confidence and reflection reinforce one another.

Over one year, Urbassik entered six sales competitions. Each strengthened a different professional skill: product knowledge, listening, quick diagnosis, strategic pacing and the ability to adapt as a conversation changed direction.

The results were visible. She placed sixth among 590 competitors at the American Marketing Association’s International Collegiate Conference and reached the top 54 at the National Collegiate Sales Competition. But rankings tell only part of the story. Internships at Fastenal and ParetoHealth let her recognize the same discovery process she had practiced in class unfolding with real clients.

ZIPD, Pi Sigma Epsilon and the American Marketing Association extended the training beyond coursework. By graduation, Urbassik had not simply collected experiences; she had connected them into a professional identity. She moved into a full-time technical sales role with Dyco Inc. prepared to plan carefully, listen closely and adapt in the moment.

Zeigler Institute for Professional Development

Fifteen years
in the room

ZIPD’s anniversary conference demonstrated a durable idea: students learn the professions faster when the professions come to them.

Students from all three Commonwealth campuses joined a program shaped around the questions changing business now—from artificial intelligence and cybersecurity to supply chain resilience, negotiation, sustainability and leadership.

The conference’s real power was proximity. Terry Zeigler ’76 and Marc Steckel ’93 joined panels. Ronn Cort, president of Dunmore, delivered the keynote. Gilberto Tito Machado ’15 and Carol Fastrich Aranos ’88 led focused talks. Alumni reviewed résumés, ran mock interviews and joined speed-networking sessions where students could test how they present themselves.

Fifteen years in, ZIPD is more than a one-day showcase. It is an operating model for career formation: repeated contact with practitioners, structured reflection and an invitation for students to practice professional behavior early and often.

New ZIPD leadership · Looking ahead

The next room
takes shape

With Cait Finn at the helm and the next ZIPD Business Conference ahead, a proven model for career readiness is entering an energetic new chapter.

Finn arrives as ZIPD’s new director with more than 15 years of experience spanning leadership development, professional coaching, higher education, athletics and organizational consulting. Her work has ranged from building leadership programs and coaching executive teams to creating curricula and connecting students with hands-on opportunities.

At Commonwealth, she will guide ZIPD across Bloomsburg, Lock Haven and Mansfield—strengthening career preparation, leadership programming, employer relationships and professional engagement. That three-campus reach gives her first year a clear purpose: make the institute’s network feel both broader and more personal for students.

The annual ZIPD Business Conference will be an early showcase for that work. Each year, hundreds of business professionals—many of them alumni—step into the role of mentor, sharing practical insight and opening conversations students can continue long after the day ends. As the next conference approaches, Finn’s background in community-building and experiential learning aligns naturally with the event’s promise: preparation becomes powerful when students can practice it with people already doing the work.

For alumni and industry partners, the conference is an invitation to return with perspective. For students, it is a chance to test questions, introductions and aspirations in a room designed to help them grow. Under new leadership, that exchange remains ZIPD’s strongest tradition—and its most promising path forward.

Centers in action

The floor becomes
the classroom

At a 586,000-square-foot distribution hub, supply chain concepts became visible, audible and immediate.

A visit organized by the Nicholas J. Giuffre Center for Supply Chain Management and the student chapter of the Association for Supply Chain Management took students inside WebstaurantStore’s Bloomsburg facility. Inventory flow, automation and warehouse operations were no longer diagrams. They were coordinated decisions happening at industrial scale.

For Morgan Lisnock, a junior double major in business management and supply chain management, the visit offered a reference point she could carry into future work. It also illustrated the role of a center: linking curriculum, student organizations and regional industry so students can compare theory with the way an operation actually runs.

Entrepreneurship & media · Lock Haven

An idea with
room to grow

The Nicholas Subich Center for Entrepreneurship and Media will give ambitious ideas a place to meet technology, mentorship and one another.

A $1.75 million gift from alumnus and entrepreneur Nicholas Subich ’17 is creating a new destination for hands-on learning at Commonwealth University–Lock Haven. The investment pairs $1 million for construction and renovation with a $750,000 commitment supporting a new faculty member—bringing space, expertise and student opportunity into one forward-looking plan.

The first phase will reimagine the ground floor of Bentley Hall as an active campus crossroads. A welcoming student lounge will make room for connection; updated classrooms with flexible furnishings and technology will support collaboration and community-facing events; and a podcast and media studio will invite students across disciplines to practice storytelling, content creation and digital communication.

A full-time director will shape programming in entrepreneurship, innovation and professional development. For business students, media students and community partners, the center promises an environment where ideas can be tested, refined and shared—and where career readiness grows naturally from making something together.

Faculty service & professional growth

Expertise
in service

Faculty leadership is most powerful when knowledge moves—into a client conversation, a new curriculum, a competition room or the next generation of colleagues.

Zeigler Consulting Services gives that movement a practical structure. Regional businesses, nonprofit organizations and public partners can work with faculty in marketing, accounting, finance, management, information technology and related fields. Students learn alongside their professors, seeing how disciplined analysis becomes an answer a real organization can use.

The exchange strengthens both sides. Community partners gain access to current expertise; students gain experience with ambiguity, expectations and teamwork; and faculty stay close to the questions reshaping the professions they teach. Consulting becomes service, applied learning and professional development at once.

The same spirit appears in program building. Professor Chulhee Jun’s work developing the new Risk Management and Insurance concentration and minor shows faculty responding to an evolving field with a new academic pathway. At career summits, sales challenges and business competitions, faculty mentors extend that work by supervising preparation, offering feedback and helping students turn performance into reflection.

Long service matters, too. The college’s recognition of accounting faculty member Dr. Mike Shapeero upon retirement celebrates the accumulated effect of years spent teaching, mentoring and strengthening a profession. New ideas and enduring service belong to the same story: faculty invest their expertise so other people can move forward.

Zeigler Consulting Services · Leadership

A bridge from
expertise to impact

As Director of Consulting Initiatives, Dr. Steve Whitehead is helping Zeigler Consulting Services connect faculty knowledge, student ambition and the real needs of regional organizations.

Commonwealth University announced Whitehead’s appointment on May 1, 2026. Made possible through grant support from the Bloomsburg University Foundation, the role gives the college dedicated leadership for expanding consulting services, strengthening business and industry partnerships and creating more workforce-aligned opportunities for students and regional employers.

Whitehead brings more than 20 years of progressive leadership across higher education, organizational innovation and business development. As associate provost of innovation at PennWest University, he led enterprise-wide strategic initiatives, launched academic programming designed for adult learners and founded an off-campus Innovation Center. At Academic Impressions, he served nationally as head of practice for academic innovation, working with higher education leaders on institutional change.

He also founded 5th Hammer Innovation, where he led consulting engagements built around practical responses to complex organizational challenges. That experience fits the promise of Zeigler Consulting Services: organizations gain thoughtful partners, faculty bring their disciplines into active practice and students learn what professional judgment looks like when the answer is not already in the back of a book.

Under Dr. Steve Whitehead, Ed.D., consulting becomes more than a service line. It becomes a bridge—linking campus expertise with regional growth, industry relationships with curriculum and today’s business questions with tomorrow’s workforce.

Business Advisory Board

The field has a seat
at the table

The board’s role is not ceremonial. It is to keep faculty, students and the business community in sustained conversation.

Commonwealth University’s official board description sets out a practical mandate: promote the college within the business community, strengthen career counseling and placement, create ongoing faculty contact with practitioners and bring professional insight into classrooms.

The membership spans sectors that shape the regional and national economy. Randy Black ’89 leads First Citizens Community Bank. Crystal Skotedis ’03 serves as CFO of Lane Enterprises. Gary Wapinski is vice president of manufacturing at Crayola. Cori Belles ’97 leads talent and experience at The Guthrie Clinic, while Richard Wisniewski brings supply chain leadership from Sanofi Pasteur.

Members serve as unpaid volunteers, normally in three-year terms. The structure matters because continuity matters: advisory work is most useful when it becomes a relationship rather than a single guest appearance. Board members can act as classroom contributors, career connectors and interpreters of changing expectations across finance, healthcare, manufacturing, technology and service.

For faculty, that access is also a form of ongoing professional exchange. Conversations with board members bring emerging practices, workforce needs and career-path insight closer to curriculum planning and classroom discussion. Students benefit from a college whose teachers remain connected to the field, while faculty gain trusted partners for testing ideas and opening doors.

Fundraising is not the board’s formal purpose, but the university notes that sustained engagement has also generated financial support for college activities. Counsel, access and philanthropy become different expressions of the same commitment: keeping the curriculum close to the work and students close to opportunity.

Alumni & giving

A career that
circles back

Tom Stiner ’76 came to Bloomsburg as a first-generation student who chose to study close to home. He launched his career at KPMG, passed the CPA exam on his first attempt and grew into CFO and COO leadership through an initial public offering and other defining business transitions.

Then experience became a resource for others. After a decade of scholarship support, Stiner expanded his service into mock interviews, résumé reviews, speed networking and classroom conversations on ethics, international business and corporate responsibility.

His story makes the alumni compact concrete: access starts the journey; achievement creates perspective; giving returns both to the students coming next.

Zeigler College of Business in Focus

Opportunity becomes capability through use

The college’s strongest stories are not about access alone. They are about what students do once they enter the room.

Global study, competition, internships, centers, alumni counsel and philanthropic support form one connected system. Students encounter the work. Faculty help them interpret it. Alumni and partners keep the work current. Donors make more encounters possible. The degree matters; what students learn to do with it matters more.
